title: Service decomposition & routing manifest (API→Orchestrator→Runtimes) - draft
body:
Purpose:
This working manifest is a short, actionable map that decomposes the control-plane surface into discrete service responsibilities and routing policy touchpoints for multi-region deployments. It is intended for platform engineers and runtime owners to reduce ambiguity when changing routing logic, onboarding new adapters, or defining upgrade boundaries.

Scope (what this doc covers):
- API gateway routing responsibilities and the minimal routing decision surface it must expose.
- Orchestration (control plane) responsibilities: policy evaluation, model variant routing, capacity tiering, and fallbacks.
- Runtime adapters (per-region/per-hardware) contract surface and failure semantics.
- Multi-region routing primitives: region preferences, geo-affinity, and cold-start fallbacks.
- SLO handoffs and telemetry expectations between layers.

Quick summary of the canonical flow (high level):
1) Client → API Gateway: performs authentication, rate-limit checks, fast path routing hinting (customer tier, region preference). Gateway annotates the request with routing metadata and forwards to the orchestrator API.
2) Orchestrator (control plane): resolves routing policy, picks a runtime adapter or pool (hosted/dedicated/private), applies model/version pinning, decides caching/kv reuse, and returns a routing token or direct proxy plan.
3) Runtime Adapter: receives token/plan, executes inference on selected GPU pool, reports metrics and traces to observability, and streams response back to gateway or client.

Core abstractions and ownership rules (recommendation):
- API Gateway (owned by eng-platform-edge):
  - Required responsibilities: auth, quota enforcement, lightweight routing hints, request validation, and connection management.
  - NOT responsible for: model selection, quantization decisions, or capacity accounting.
  - Contract: include X-Routing-Meta header with {customer-tier, region-hint, model-family, request-id}. Keep header schema stable (versioned).

- Orchestrator / Control Plane (owned by eng-platform-orchestration):
  - Required responsibilities: deterministic policy evaluation, region failover logic, model variant resolution, rollout evaluation (canary vs baseline), and final routing token issuance.
  - Exposes: /v1/route-plan API (stateless) that returns plan-id, pool-id, adapter-type, and a short-lived signing token for runtimes.
  - Data owned: policy definitions, route metrics, model inventory, and rollout configurations.

- Runtime Adapters (owned by runtime teams or infra stewards per region):
  - Required responsibilities: accept plan-id, validate token, execute inference, manage kv-cache lifecycle, emit L4/L7 metrics, and implement backpressure semantics.
  - Adapter surface: init/handshake, execute(request, params), health/probe endpoints, and an event stream for token revocation or configuration updates.
  - Failure semantics: adapters must be able to declare transient (retryable) vs permanent (failover) errors and provide a suggested retry-backoff policy.

Ownership matrix (principles to follow):
- Single owner per logical capability (auth, policy-eval, model-catalog) unless explicitly cross-owned.
- Owning team must publish a 1-page handoff doc and a conformance test harness in GH.
- Changes that expand routing surface (new headers, token formats) require cross-team announcement + 2-week deprecation period.

Routing policy primitives (policy DSL sketch):
- match(customer_id) -> prefer(dedicated) else best-effort(hosted)
- prefer(region=EU) unless latency > 200ms -> fallback(region=NA)
- pin(model=redwood-13b, quant=8bit) if customer_tier in (enterprise)
- canary(percent=5, metric=latency_p50) with auto-fallback on regression

Multi-region considerations and fallbacks:
- Geo-affinity: default routing should respect customer region preference; explicit flag (allow_cross_region) can override for cost/latency optimization.
- Cold-start mitigation: orchestrator should prefer adapters with warm cache for cache-sensitive workloads; maintain a small warm pool per region for premium customers.
- Cross-region SLOs: define two separate SLO buckets — within-region latency SLO and cross-region (fallback) SLO. Both must be tracked per-customer.

Observability and SLO handoffs (what to emit and who owns it):
- Gateway emits ingress latency, auth failures, and per-route request counts (owner: platform-edge).
- Orchestrator emits policy-decision latency, plan issuance rate, and reasons for fallback (owner: platform-orchestration).
- Adapter emits execution latency, token validation failures, cache hit-rate, GPU-utilization, and tail-p99 (owner: runtime-adapter team).
- Trace Propagation: each segment must include plan-id and pool-id to correlate across systems.

Rollout and upgrade contract between teams:
- All control-plane components follow: canary → gradual traffic ramp → full rollout. For routing policy changes, default a feature-flag off and do phased enablement per-customer.
- Adapter spec versioning: adapters must declare supported spec-version in handshake and be forward compatible with +1 minor version.
- Automated conformance: PRs that touch routing path must run the route-sim harness (GH action) that asserts no regressions on a predefined set of traffic profiles.

Failure modes, recommended mitigations, and runbook pointers:
- Orchestrator outage: fallback to last-known-good static routing table for critical customers (owned by platform-orchestration).
- Adapter region degradation: orchestrator should mark pool as degraded and trigger automated cross-region failover for eligible requests; notify on-call via PagerDuty.
- Token signing key rotation: rotate keys in a staged manner using key-version headers; adapters must accept previous version for a grace period.

Open questions / tradeoffs (callouts for architecture discussion):
- How much decisioning should live in the gateway vs orchestrator? (tradeoff: gateway low-latency vs orchestrator central policy governance).
- Should plan issuance be synchronous (blocking) or async streaming token to gateway? (sync simpler to reason about; async reduces gateway load).
- Do we allow runtime adapters to perform last-mile batching/aggregation decisions, or must batching be driven by orchestrator?

Immediate next steps / TODOs (owners assigned):
- (Aisha) Draft minimal plan-id schema and publish in GH (PR target: 2025-02-10).
- (Ravi) Prototype route-sim harness for cross-region failover scenarios (JIRA-2147).
- (Liam) Adapter handshake proto draft and health semantics doc (target: 2025-02-18).
- (Maya) Update observability dashboards to include plan-id as a primary filter (ticket: DASH-86).

Notes to self / informal:
- Keep this doc intentionally concise. The goal is a single-pane starting point that links into deeper design docs per component.
- Expect many iterations; tag items that require legal/security review (data residency controls) before any customer-facing changes.

Appendix: quick glossary of fields used in headers/plan tokens:
- plan-id: opaque routing id emitted by orchestrator
- pool-id: logical runtime pool (region+hardware+config)
- model-family: human-readable model catalog id
- spec-version: routing plan schema version

References and context links: see linked_artifacts above and the related platform roadmaps in Confluence.

End of manifest (v0.1 draft).
